questions.questionText: Under IAS 16 (Property, Plant and Equipment), when a non-current asset with a carrying amount of $48,000 is revalued upward to $65,000, how is the $17,000 revaluation surplus initially recognised?

options.text: Credited to Other Comprehensive Income and accumulated in a Revaluation Reserve in Equity
Credited immediately to Operating Profit in the Statement of Profit or Loss
Credited to Trade Payables as a deferred liability
Debited to Accumulated Depreciation only without changing Equity

questions.explanation: IAS 16 requires a first-time revaluation surplus to be recognised in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) and credited to the Revaluation Reserve within Equity (not in profit or loss unless reversing a previous revaluation loss).

questions.questionText: Under IAS 2 (Inventories), inventory items have historical cost $14,200, estimated selling price $15,000, and necessary selling & completion costs of $1,600. At what value must the inventory be stated?
questions.explanation: NRV = Selling price ($15,000) − Costs to sell ($1,600) = $13,400. IAS 2 mandates inventory be valued at the lower of Cost ($14,200) and NRV ($13,400) = $13,400.

questions.questionText: Under IAS 10 (Events after the Reporting Period), a major credit customer owing $22,000 at 31 December 2025 is declared bankrupt on 18 January 2026 before the financial statements are authorised. How is this treated?

options.text: Ignore completely until the 2026 financial statements
Non-adjusting event: disclose by note only without changing 2025 profit
Adjusting event: write off the irrecoverable debt against 2025 profit and Trade Receivables
Transfer the debt directly to the Share Premium account

questions.explanation: A customer bankruptcy soon after year-end normally confirms conditions (credit weakness) already existing at the reporting date, so IAS 10 classifies it as an adjusting event.

questions.questionText: Which transaction appears under Cash Flows from Financing Activities in a Statement of Cash Flows prepared under IAS 7?

options.text: Cash received from trade receivables
Cash paid to suppliers for inventory purchases
Proceeds from the disposal of old delivery machinery
Proceeds from a new issue of ordinary shares and repayment of a 10% debenture loan

questions.explanation: IAS 7 defines Financing Activities as those altering the size and composition of contributed equity and borrowings (share issues, share redemptions, debenture/loan receipts & repayments).

questions.questionText: Under IAS 37 (Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets), when a legal claim against a company is judged "possible" (less than 50% probability, not remote), how should it be treated?

options.text: Disclosed as a contingent liability in the notes to the financial statements
Recognised as a liability on the Statement of Financial Position
Recognised as a contingent asset in revenue
Written off against the Capital Redemption Reserve

questions.explanation: Under IAS 37: Probable (>50%) present obligation = recognise a Provision; Possible obligation = disclose as Contingent Liability in notes; Remote = ignore.

questions.questionText: When a partnership admits a new partner and decides NOT to keep a Goodwill account in the books, how is Goodwill (say $30,000, old PSR 2:1, new PSR 2:2:1) adjusted?

options.text: Debit old partners in old ratio and credit the bank account
Credit old partners in old ratio ($20,000; $10,000) and debit all partners in new ratio ($12,000; $12,000; $6,000)
Credit Goodwill permanently as a current asset
Divide Goodwill equally among old and new partners regardless of PSR

questions.explanation: Raising Goodwill credits old partners in their old PSR; writing off Goodwill debits all partners in the new PSR — resulting in a net transfer from gaining to sacrificing partners.

questions.questionText: Under the rule in Garner v Murray upon partnership dissolution when one partner is insolvent, how do the solvent partners share the insolvent partner's capital deficiency?

options.text: In the old profit-sharing ratio only
Equally regardless of capital or profit-sharing ratios
In the ratio of their last agreed capital balances before dissolution
In proportion to drawings made during the final year

questions.explanation: Under Garner v Murray, solvent partners bring in cash equal to their share of realisation loss and bear the insolvent partner's capital deficiency in the ratio of their last agreed capitals.

questions.questionText: A limited company makes a 1-for-4 bonus issue of $1 ordinary shares using Share Premium ($40,000) and Retained Earnings, based on 200,000 existing shares. What happens to Total Equity?

options.text: Non-current liabilities increase by $50,000
Total Equity increases by $50,000 and Cash increases by $50,000
Total Equity decreases by $50,000 as dividends are paid
Total Equity remains unchanged because reserves are capitalised into Share Capital

questions.explanation: Bonus shares are issued free to existing shareholders by transferring reserves to Share Capital (Dr Share Premium/Retained Earnings, Cr Share Capital). Cash and Total Equity do not change.

questions.questionText: Why does a manufacturing enterprise create a Provision for Unrealised Profit on manufactured finished goods inventory?

options.text: To eliminate internal factory profit on unsold goods so closing inventory is stated at production cost in the SOFP
To inflate net profit before declaration of dividends
To evade corporate income tax on factory overhead
To record depreciation on raw materials

questions.explanation: Under prudence/realisation, profit cannot be recognised until goods are sold to an external customer. Eliminating factory mark-up on unsold finished goods prevents overstating inventory and profit.

questions.questionText: A manufacturing company transfers finished goods at cost plus 25% factory mark-up. Unsold finished goods at transfer price increased from $20,000 to $30,000. What is the charge to the Income Statement?

options.text: $2,500 expense
$2,000 expense (increase in provision for unrealised profit)
$10,000 revenue
$2,000 credit to profit

questions.explanation: Mark-up 25% on cost = margin 25/125 = 1/5 (20%) on transfer price. Opening PUP = $4,000; Closing PUP = $6,000. Increase = $2,000 debited to Profit or Loss.

questions.questionText: Which journal entry records the redemption of $100,000 of redeemable preference shares out of Retained Earnings where no new shares are issued?

options.text: Dr Revaluation Reserve $100k, Cr Preference Share Capital $100k
Dr Share Premium $100k, Cr Cash $100k
Dr Preference Share Capital $100k, Cr Bank $100k; and Dr Retained Earnings $100k, Cr Capital Redemption Reserve $100k
Dr Bank $100k, Cr Retained Earnings $100k

questions.explanation: When redeemable shares are redeemed without fresh share proceeds, an equivalent sum must be transferred from distributable profits (Retained Earnings) to a non-distributable Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) to maintain capital.

questions.questionText: A company's EPS is $0.45 and market price per ordinary share is $3.60. Calculate the Price/Earnings (P/E) ratio and state what it indicates.

options.text: 4.05 times — gearing multiple
0.125 times — dividend payout proportion
12.5% — earnings yield only
8.0 times — investors pay $8 for each $1 of current annual earnings per share

questions.explanation: P/E ratio = Market price per share ÷ EPS = $3.60 ÷ $0.45 = 8.0 times, reflecting market expectations of future earnings growth and risk.

questions.questionText: If a business has Dividend Cover of 2.5 times and Profit After Tax of $125,000 (no preference shares), what total ordinary dividend was declared?
questions.explanation: Dividend Cover = Profit available to ordinary shareholders ÷ Total Ordinary Dividend. Thus Ordinary Dividend = $125,000 ÷ 2.5 = $50,000.

questions.questionText: Under IAS 36 (Impairment of Assets), an asset has carrying amount $90,000, fair value less costs of disposal $72,000, and value in use $78,000. What is the impairment loss?
questions.explanation: Recoverable amount = higher of Fair Value Less Costs of Disposal ($72,000) and Value in Use ($78,000) = $78,000. Impairment loss = Carrying amount ($90,000) − $78,000 = $12,000.

questions.questionText: In cost accounting, when production volume exceeds sales volume during a period, how does Absorption Costing profit compare with Marginal Costing profit (assuming constant unit costs)?

options.text: Both methods report identical net profit in every accounting period
Marginal Costing always shows a higher profit because fixed overheads are deferred
Absorption Costing shows a higher profit because part of fixed production overhead is carried forward in closing inventory
Absorption Costing shows a lower profit due to variable selling costs

questions.explanation: When inventory rises (Production > Sales), Absorption Costing absorbs a share of fixed factory overhead into closing inventory valuation, reducing cost of sales and raising reported profit relative to Marginal Costing.

questions.questionText: Standard material per unit is 4 kg at $5/kg. Actual output of 1,000 units used 4,300 kg costing $20,640 (actual price $4.80/kg). What are the Material Price Variance and Material Usage Variance?

options.text: Price Variance $640 (A); Usage Variance $1,500 (F)
Price Variance $1,500 (A); Usage Variance $860 (F)
Price Variance $800 (F); Usage Variance $1,440 (A)
Price Variance $860 (F); Usage Variance $1,500 (A)

questions.explanation: Price variance = AQ(SP − AP) = 4,300($5.00 − $4.80) = $860 Favourable. Usage variance = SP(SQ − AQ) = $5(4,000 − 4,300) = $1,500 Adverse. Net total = $640 Adverse.

questions.questionText: Standard labour is 2 hours/unit at $8/hour. Actual output is 500 units taking 950 hours at a total wage cost of $8,075. Calculate the Labour Rate and Labour Efficiency Variances.

options.text: Rate Variance $475 (A); Efficiency Variance $400 (F)
Rate Variance $400 (F); Efficiency Variance $475 (A)
Rate Variance $500 (A); Efficiency Variance $425 (F)
Rate Variance $75 (A); Efficiency Variance $475 (F)

questions.explanation: Standard hours for 500 units = 1,000 hrs. Actual wage cost $8,075 vs standard cost for 950 hrs ($7,600) → Rate Variance = $475 Adverse. Efficiency Variance = $8(1,000 − 950) = $400 Favourable.

questions.questionText: A product sells at $40/unit, variable cost is $24/unit, and fixed costs are $96,000. If actual sales are 8,000 units, what is the Margin of Safety in units and as a percentage of actual sales?
questions.explanation: Contribution/unit = $40 − $24 = $16. Break-even = $96,000 ÷ $16 = 6,000 units. Margin of Safety = 8,000 − 6,000 = 2,000 units; 2,000 ÷ 8,000 = 25%.

questions.questionText: Three products require a single scarce machine-hour bottleneck: Product X (Contribution $30, 3 machine hrs), Product Y ($24, 2 machine hrs), Product Z ($28, 4 machine hrs). Which ranking maximises profit?

options.text: Z ($7/hr), then X ($10/hr), then Y ($12/hr)
Y ($12/hr), then X ($10/hr), then Z ($7/hr)
X ($10/hr), then Y ($12/hr), then Z ($7/hr)

questions.explanation: With a limiting factor, rank by contribution per unit of scarce resource: Y = $24/2 = $12/hr; X = $30/3 = $10/hr; Z = $28/4 = $7/hr.

questions.questionText: In Capital Investment Appraisal, which statement accurately describes the Internal Rate of Return (IRR)?

options.text: The weighted average cost of equity and preference capital only
The average annual accounting profit divided by initial capital outlay
The number of years required to recover the undiscounted initial outlay
The discount rate at which the Net Present Value (NPV) of a project equals zero

questions.explanation: IRR is the discount rate (cost of capital) where Present Value of cash inflows equals Present Value of cash outflows (NPV = 0). A project is accepted when IRR exceeds the firm's cost of capital.

questions.questionText: Under Activity-Based Costing (ABC), what is a "cost driver"?

options.text: A factor or activity (such as machine setups, purchase orders, or inspections) that causes overhead costs to be incurred
The direct wage rate paid to factory supervisors
The depreciation method chosen under IAS 16
Total fixed selling and distribution expenses

questions.explanation: ABC groups overheads into cost pools and assigns them to products using cost drivers—the measurable activities causing each pool's cost to vary.

questions.questionText: Under IAS 8 (Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors), how is a change in the useful life of a depreciable machine treated?

options.text: As a change in accounting policy: applied retrospectively by restating prior-year comparative statements
As a change in accounting estimate: applied prospectively to current and future periods
Written off directly to Share Premium
Treated as an extraordinary prior-period error

questions.explanation: Changing asset useful life or residual value is a change in accounting estimate (IAS 8) and is accounted for prospectively in current and future periods.

questions.questionText: A company owes $200,000 in 8% debentures and has $300,000 in Share Capital & Reserves. Total Capital Employed is $500,000 and PBIT is $75,000. What are the Capital Gearing Ratio and Interest Cover?

options.text: Gearing = 25%; Interest Cover = 10 times
Gearing = 66.7%; Interest Cover = 2.5 times
Gearing = 40% (Debt/Total Capital Employed); Interest Cover = 4.69 times
Gearing = 40%; Interest Cover = 9.38 times

questions.explanation: Gearing = Fixed-cost capital / Total Capital Employed = $200,000 / $500,000 = 40%. Annual interest = 8% × $200,000 = $16,000. Interest cover = PBIT / Interest = $75,000 / $16,000 = 4.69 times.

questions.questionText: Why might a business experience a cash shortage even while reporting strong net profit?

options.text: Trade payables refused cash discounts
Depreciation expense reduced net cash inflow during the period
Share premium was credited instead of retained earnings
Rapid sales growth tied up cash in higher trade receivables and inventory, or heavy capital expenditure and loan repayments occurred

questions.explanation: Profit (accrual basis) differs from cash: working capital absorption (rising debtors/stock), asset purchases, tax/dividends paid, and loan repayments reduce cash without lowering operating profit; depreciation reduces profit without using cash.

questions.questionText: In a Make-or-Buy short-term decision where spare capacity exists, which costs are relevant to manufacturing a component in-house?

options.text: Incremental variable manufacturing costs plus any avoidable specific fixed costs attributable to the component
Apportioned general factory rent and head-office administration salaries
Historical sunk development costs incurred two years ago
Book value depreciation of existing idle machinery

questions.explanation: Only future, incremental, differential cash flows (direct materials, direct labour, variable overhead, avoidable fixed costs, and any opportunity cost) are relevant; sunk and general absorbed fixed costs are irrelevant.

questions.questionText: Under IAS 38 (Intangible Assets), how must internal Research expenditure versus qualifying Development expenditure be treated?

options.text: Capitalise both Research and Development costs indefinitely without amortisation
Expense Research costs immediately in profit or loss; capitalise Development costs only if all six strict IAS 38 commercial/technical feasibility criteria are met
Expense Development costs and capitalise all Research costs as Goodwill
Recognise both inside Inventory at NRV

questions.explanation: IAS 38 requires all Research expenditure to be expensed as incurred, while Development expenditure is capitalised as an intangible asset only when technical feasibility, intention/ability to use or sell, probable future benefits, resources, and reliable measurement are demonstrated.

questions.questionText: A machine costs $50,000 (no residual value, 5-year life). Annual net cash inflows are $16,000. What is the Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) based on initial investment?

options.text: 12% [($16,000 − $10,000 depreciation) = $6,000 average profit ÷ $50,000]

questions.explanation: Annual depreciation = $50,000 ÷ 5 = $10,000. Average accounting profit = Cash flow ($16,000) − Depreciation ($10,000) = $6,000/yr. ARR = ($6,000 ÷ $50,000) × 100% = 12%.

questions.questionText: Budgeted fixed production overhead was $60,000 for 12,000 budgeted labour hours (10,000 units). Actual output was 10,500 units using 12,400 hours and actual fixed overhead was $61,500. What is the Fixed Overhead Expenditure Variance?

options.text: $1,000 Adverse
$3,000 Favourable
$1,500 Favourable
$1,500 Adverse ($60,000 budgeted − $61,500 actual)

questions.explanation: Fixed Overhead Expenditure Variance = Budgeted Fixed Overhead ($60,000) − Actual Fixed Overhead ($61,500) = $1,500 Adverse (overspent).

questions.questionText: In budgetary control, why is a Flexible Budget essential for performance evaluation?

options.text: It adjusts budgeted variable costs and revenues to the actual level of activity achieved so true operational efficiency variances are isolated
It eliminates the need to record actual expenditure in the ledger
It guarantees zero variance at the end of every financial year
It converts absorption costing statements into cash flow statements

questions.explanation: Comparing actual costs at 12,000 units against a static budget for 10,000 units mixes volume changes with efficiency. Flexing the budget to 12,000 units isolates real price/efficiency performance.

questions.questionText: In incomplete records, opening inventory is $18,000, closing inventory is $22,000, purchases are $124,000, and sales achieve a uniform 20% gross profit margin on sales. Calculate Total Sales.
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = $18,000 + $124,000 − $22,000 = $120,000. Since Margin = 20% of Sales, COGS = 80% of Sales → Sales = $120,000 ÷ 0.80 = $150,000.
